chapter: The 1949 band, breakup and later years
title: Clark Terry's style, friendship and drawings
summary: Barnet says Terry sounded the same then as now, came from George Hudson's band, and remains a close friend; Willard recalls Terry's sketches of the Ellington band.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Did Clarke have a set style -- not a set style, but I mean an identifiable style?
Oh, that's the way he sounds today, the same way.
Because I wasn't aware of him that early, and --
George Hudson's band he came out of, in St. Louis.
I know he's from St. Louis.
How long did Clarke stay with you?

Oh, he was with me about a year then. Maybe longer than that. Clarke I count as one of my dearest and closest friends. We're in touch all the time. I hear from him from all over the world and we get on the phone every now and then and just talk.

He sends me postcards with -- whenever I see him he always says, 'Hi, Pat,' on his trumpet, you know, not speaking, but speaks through his horn. And so I get cards from all over the world with the bell of a trumpet and, 'Hi, Pat,' coming out of it.
Oh, he's very busy with those cards.

Oh, he's quite an artist. I -- one of the -- one set of drawings made an impression on me, I'll never forget, and I keep asking him, you know, 'Where are they?' Duke was rehearsing at [Lewisohn] Stadium, and this was 1958, and I was wandering around the stage, taking pictures of the band, and I walked -- this was only rehearsal, and I could do that -- walked back behind the trumpet section, looked over Clarke's shoulder, and Clarke was drawing everybody in the band, but the trumpet's eye view. It's the way Quentin Clinton Jackson looked from behind, spilling over the side of the seat.
The way Paul Gonsalves Gonzalez looked asleep in his chair, from the angle of in the trumpet section. Shorty Baker taking a solo at the microphone, from behind.
